title: Rogue Domain Controller
summary: A rogue domain controller is a machine that an adversary registers in Active Directory so that it appears to be a legitimate replica of the domain directory. The machine is added by creating new server and directory service agent objects in the Configuration partition of the directory schema, which requires domain administrator rights, local administrator rights on a controller, or the KRBTGT password hash. Once registered, the fake controller can push changes into the real directory, including object attributes, access control lists and schema data, and it can receive replication traffic that ordinary monitoring does not watch. Because that replication happens outside normal audit paths, central log collection may record nothing at all. Detection therefore depends on change auditing and replication metadata: new or re-enabled server objects, replication from unexpected source addresses, spikes in directory attribute changes, and the sudden appearance of history attributes on accounts. Legitimate promotion of a new controller is planned change work with a matching computer account lifecycle.

beginner.definition: A domain controller is the server that holds the list of users and computers for a network. A rogue domain controller is a fake one that an attacker adds to that list. The network then trusts it like a real server. It can quietly change records without normal alarms.
beginner.whyItMatters: The directory server is the heart of a Windows network. If an attacker controls a fake one, they can change passwords, add secret accounts and hide their actions. Many alarms never fire, because the fake server does not report to normal monitors. This can give an attacker a permanent way back in. It also makes later investigation much harder, because records may be altered or deleted.
howItWorks: The attacker needs very high rights, such as domain administrator, or the secret key of the domain.
They create new objects in the directory that describe a server and its directory service agent.
The directory now treats this machine as a real replica of the domain database.
The fake server receives and sends directory copies, which normal monitors often ignore.
It can then change any object, including accounts, group settings and permission lists.
Finally it may clean up its own traces by removing replication records and history data.
beginner.example: Picture a hospital where every ward keeps patient notes in one central registry. A manager with a master key adds a new office to the building list. The registry software starts sending that office copies of every note, because it looks like a real records office. The office can then edit any patient file, add a fake patient, or delete an entry. Nobody at the front desk notices, because the fake office never appears on the visitor log. It never has to ask for permission either.
takeaways: A fake domain controller can change the directory without appearing in normal security logs.
Watch for new or re-enabled server objects and for replication from unexpected machines.
Very high rights, or the domain secret key, are needed, so protect them carefully.

objectives: Explain what a rogue domain controller is and why it can modify directory data.
Describe the directory objects an attacker creates to register a fake controller.
Identify the audit and replication metadata that reveals an unexpected replica.
Explain why replication from a rogue controller may be invisible to central log collection.
Describe how this technique supports backdoors and history attribute abuse.
